en: The Sūtra on the Kātyāyana of the Veṇu Clan.
Wal_1: "Ask, sister; having heard it, I shall explain it to you.
Wal_2: "O Śramaṇa, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who maintain that pleasure and pain are created by oneself. There are... [they exist].

Some designate pleasure and pain as created by another; some designate them as both self-created and created by another; and some designate pleasure and pain as arising without being created by oneself or by another, but through causes. How do the Arhats designate pleasure and pain as they arise?
The Arhats designate pleasure and pain as arising in a different manner.
“Monk, how is it that the Arhats designate pleasure and pain as having arisen otherwise?
“Sister, the Arhats designate pleasure and pain as dependently originated.
“Monk, how is it that the Arhats designate pleasure and pain as dependently originated?”
"In that case, sister, I shall question you; answer as you see fit.

What do you think, sister? Is there an eye? ‘There is, ascetic. Is there form? ‘There is, ascetic. Sister, if an eye were to arise, would there, conditioned by eye-contact, arise internally a feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant?”
"There is, O Śramaṇa, the ear; there is the nose; there is the tongue; there is the body; there is the mind.
There is, O Śramaṇa, [the category of] phenomena."

“If there were ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and they were to arise, would there, conditioned by the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, arise internally a feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant? “There would, ascetic.”
"Thus indeed, sister, do the Arhats designate pleasure and pain as dependently originated.

Thus indeed, ascetic, do the Arhats designate pleasure as dependently originated. How then, ascetic, do the Arhats designate the cessation of pleasure and pain? "In that case, sister, I shall question you; answer this as it seems right to you."
"What do you think, sister? If, sister, the eye were to cease entirely, in every way and without remainder,

and were to go to total disappearance, dissolution, and exhaustion without remainder, would there still arise internally, conditioned by eye-contact, a feeling— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant?"
"No, Śramaṇa. Sister, if the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind were to cease entirely, in every way and without remainder,
and were to go to total destruction, disappearance, and exhaustion without remainder, would there still be [feeling] conditioned by mind-contact?"
“Sister, internally there arises a feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
“No, ascetic.
“For it is in this way, sister, that Arhats declare the cessation of pleasure and pain as they have arisen through dependent origination.”

While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose in her, who belonged to the clan of Veṇukātyāyana. Then, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma, she crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, became independent of others, and no longer led by others; having attained confidence in the Teacher’s instruction regarding the phenomena, she stood firm.
Rising from his seat, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the venerable Udāyin, he said this to the venerable Udāyin:
"I have gone beyond, O ascetic; I have gone beyond. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks."
"And, O Śramaṇa, accept me as a female lay follower (upāsikā), who from this day forward for as long as life lasts has gone for refuge with my very life and is full of faith.
Then Udāyin, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Brahmin woman of the Veṇukātyāyana clan with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
